Article Title: 'Left' in existential crisis: From CPI-CPM rift in Kerala to Delhi rout, old fault lines deepen
Article Text:
The Left faces a deeper political challenge as electoral setbacks, internal tensions and shrinking influence converge

Pinarayi probe: Another challenge after Kerala defeat

DUSU polls: Why isn't Left mobilisation becoming votes?

CPI vs CPM: When opposition itself becomes a battlefield

From Bengal to Kerala: How did the Left reach here?

What next for the Left?

There was a time when the Left’s political footprint stretched from West Bengal to Tripura and Kerala. Its influence travelled further still, through trade unions, university campuses, farmers’ movements and a cadre network that kept the red flag visible even where Communist parties were not in power. That map has steadily grown smaller.For India’s Left, the question is no longer only about shrinking electoral numbers. It is increasingly about where the Communist movement still has the political space, organisational confidence and social influence to assert itself. In Delhi, the SFI-AISA alliance has struggled to translate visible participation in student mobilisations into votes. In Kerala, the two principal constituents of the Left Democratic Front, the CPM and CPI, have found themselves publicly at odds over even the distribution of positions within the opposition, and that too after a heavy defeat in the assembly elections.These may appear to be separate battles, but they have come at a particularly difficult moment for the Left. The Kerala defeat has left it without a state government, the CPM and CPI are publicly disagreeing over the way forward, former chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan is facing a probe, and the Delhi university results have again exposed the gap between the Left’s visibility in student movements and its electoral reach.The timing makes these developments particularly significant. The Left’s retreat has been a long process. The fall of the Left Front in West Bengal in 2011, the loss of Tripura in 2018 and the steady decline in its parliamentary strength had already reduced the Communist parties’ national footprint. Kerala had remained the exception, a state where the Left retained a durable organisational network and, in 2021, even broke the state’s established cycle of alternating between the LDF and UDF governments. Its defeat in 2026 means that India currently has no state government led by a Communist party.But the more revealing question may be what is happening beneath the election results. Is the Left merely going through another electoral trough, particularly after a decade in power in Kerala, or are the latest developments exposing older fault lines, from leadership and alliance tensions to the difficulty of converting traditional political mobilisation into electoral support?On September 22, the UDF government ordered a police inquiry based on an Enforcement Directorate report concerning allegations involving former chief minister and current leader of opposition Pinarayi Vijayan, his daughter Veena T and son-in-law PA Mohammed Riyas in the CMRL-Exalogic case. The state government said the inquiry would be entrusted to the state police; reports said it would initially be conducted by the Crime Branch without registration of an FIR.The underlying allegations are already part of an ED investigation. The agency has alleged financial irregularities involving payments made by Cochin Minerals and Rutile Ltd to Veena's now-defunct company Exalogic Solutions, and has sought action against Vijayan and others. The Kerala government's decision followed legal advice on whether the information and material supplied by the ED warranted a preliminary inquiry.For the CPM, however, the political dimension is inseparable from the legal one. Party general secretary MA Baby has said the party will fight the matter “legally and politically”, while accusing central agencies of having been used against opposition leaders.That places the Left in an unfamiliar position in Kerala. For a decade, Vijayan and the CPM were operating from government. Now the former chief minister is leading the opposition while facing a probe ordered by the government that replaced him.The probe comes only months after the LDF lost power following a decade in government, at a time when the CPM is already examining what went wrong and trying to regroup in opposition. The question is therefore not simply whether the allegations withstand investigation. The episode also puts Vijayan and the record of the previous government back under scrutiny at a particularly difficult moment for the party.The Delhi University Students' Union election offers a different window into the Left's problem, particularly its ability to convert activism and issue-based mobilisation into electoral support.The SFI-AISA alliance had been visible in campaigns around issues including student housing, examinations and accountability, and had participated prominently in the CJP mobilisation. Yet its electoral numbers declined in three of the four central-panel contests compared with 2025. Its presidential candidate Ananya Raturi received 5,377 votes, almost identical to the 5,385 polled by the alliance's candidate last year. But its vice-presidential tally fell from 4,163 to 2,383, the secretary vote from 9,535 to 8,734 and the joint-secretary vote from 8,425 to 5,837.The results also showed that student politics cannot simply be read as a binary contest between the major national parties and the Left. ABVP won three of the four central-panel positions, while Independent candidate Deepanshu Shokeen won the vice-president's post with 30,615 votes. He had previously been associated with Congress-affiliated NSUI but contested independently after not receiving its ticket.For the Left, the striking element is the gap between mobilisation and electoral conversion. A political organisation can be prominent in protests, articulate grievances on campuses and participate in wider movements, but that visibility does not automatically translate into votes.The presidential contest is particularly revealing. The Left candidate finished with 5,377 votes, while ABVP's Yash Dabas won with 24,576 and NSUI's Vijay Shankar Meena polled 22,523. The result does not erase the Left's presence on campus, but it does expose the difficulty of turning that presence into control of student institutions.And that is why the DUSU result matters beyond one university election. Student politics has historically been an important space for the Left to recruit, organise and build its next generation of political workers. Sitaram Yechury, for instance, rose through student politics at JNU before eventually becoming CPI(M) general secretary.The question for the Left now is simpler: if it can still bring young people to protests and movements, why is it struggling to bring them to the ballot box?The strain is also visible inside Kerala's Left alliance. After the LDF's assembly defeat, the CPI demanded the post of deputy leader of the opposition in the assembly, arguing for a larger role within the alliance. The CPM, however, rejected the demand, with Vijayan publicly opposing it.On the surface, the disagreement is about a post. But underneath it is a larger debate about how the LDF should function after its election defeat. The CPI has argued for greater sharing of responsibilities and “collective leadership”, while the CPM has maintained that the alliance should follow its established conventions.The disagreement soon spilled into public. CPI state secretary Binoy Viswam criticised Vijayan's stand, while senior CPI leader C Divakaran went further and questioned Vijayan's authority to dismiss the demand. Divakaran also argued that Vijayan should have taken responsibility for the election defeat rather than becoming leader of the opposition.The CPM pushed back too. CPM state secretariat member C N Mohanan questioned the CPI's electoral strength and accused it of using pressure tactics against the larger ally.The dispute may appear procedural because the deputy leader's post is largely an organisational and parliamentary position. But its political significance lies elsewhere. The CPI has sought greater recognition after the LDF's defeat, while the CPM, as the dominant force in the alliance, remains the principal party responsible for its direction.The two parties have since tried to prevent the dispute from escalating further. But the episode illustrates a problem that often becomes sharper after an electoral defeat: who takes responsibility for the loss, and who gets to decide the course correction?Kerala's 2026 verdict completed a long retreat. West Bengal's Left Front had ruled continuously from 1977 until 2011, while Tripura remained under Left Front rule for 25 years before the BJP ended that run in 2018. Kerala subsequently became the Left's last major governing base.But the story of the Left's decline has not been the same everywhere. In West Bengal, the 2011 defeat ended 34 years of uninterrupted Left Front rule and the Communist parties have since struggled to recover their old electoral space. In Tripura, the BJP displaced the Left after 25 years in power and emerged as its principal rival. Kerala followed a different trajectory, with power traditionally alternating between the LDF and Congress-led UDF.That is what made the LDF's 2021 victory particularly significant. The Vijayan government returned for a second consecutive term, breaking Kerala's four-decade pattern of alternating governments and giving the Left something it no longer had elsewhere: a state where it could demonstrate that it remained capable not only of surviving, but of retaining power.The 2026 defeat is therefore different from Bengal and Tripura and cannot automatically be equated with the organisational collapse witnessed elsewhere. Yet the scale of the setback raises questions beyond normal anti-incumbency. The LDF was reduced from 94 seats to 35, while the UDF won 102. The CPI(M) also suffered defeats in areas traditionally associated with its organisation, including parts of Kannur. BJP candidates won three seats, Chathannoor, Nemom and Kazhakoottam, including constituencies that had been held by LDF leaders.The larger national trajectory has been just as stark. At its parliamentary peak in 2004, the Left parties together had 59 Lok Sabha MPs and provided crucial outside support to the first UPA government. Twenty-two years later, their presence in Parliament and across state governments is a fraction of what it was.The decline cannot be traced to a single election or a single cause. The Left has had to contend with the loss of old strongholds, changes in the nature of work and organised labour, the rise of powerful regional parties, the BJP's expansion into states where the Left once had substantial space, and the challenge of reaching a generation of voters with little memory of the Communist parties at the height of their political influence.Kerala had, for years, stood apart from that national decline. The 2026 result does not mean the Left's organisational base in the state has disappeared, but it has removed its last seat of state power and made the problems elsewhere much harder to ignore.With no Communist-led state government left, a diminished parliamentary presence, weaker conversion of student mobilisation into votes and visible friction among its own principal parties, the Left finds itself at one of its most difficult political moments.The challenge is no longer simply how to win the next election. It is whether the political space that once made the Communist movement a national force can still be reconstructed, and whether the Left can address its old fault lines while finding its place in a changing political landscape.
Article Summary: India's Left faces a deeper political challenge as electoral setbacks, internal tensions and shrinking influence converge. The Kerala defeat has left it without a state government, the CPM and CPI are publicly disagreeing over the way forward, and former chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan is facing a probe. Delhi university results have again exposed the gap between the Left’s visibility in student movements and its electoral reach.

Article Title: New Form 6 enrolments where no SIR is under way won't need mapping
Article Text:
EC retains mandatory SIR declaration for fresh voter enrolment.

NEW DELHI: Those applying for fresh enrolment as electors through Form 6 in locations other than the 12 states and UTs where special intensive revision (SIR) is currently underway will no longer need to attach a declaration mapping themselves or their relative to the electoral rolls from the last SIR.In the states and UTs where SIR is going on, Form 6 will continue to be accompanied by a mandatory declaration by the applicant listing their or their relatives' electoral rolls details from the last SIR, apart from their father's, mother's and spouse's names and their respective EPIC numbers, if available.A statement put out by the three-member Election Commission Saturday justified the continued requirement of new electors to submit the declaration along with Form 6 as part of SIR, saying "the declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Supreme Court ".For the non-SIR period, the forms applicable as per the Registration of Electors Rules 1960 will be used, the commission added. The declaration was first added to Form 6 in the SIR order issued for Bihar on June 24, 2025.Sources told TOI the system will revert to the pre-SIR Form 6 with immediate effect in non-SIR states/UTs, including the states due for polls early next year.As exclusively reported by TOI on Sept 25, a special summary revision will be undertaken in these poll-bound states later this year.Both election commissioners, SS Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had in May and Aug, respectively, sent internal notes to the deputy election commissioner concerned, opining that Form 6 can only be amended by the govt.This was after they had approved of the declaration attached to the form as part of three SIR orders. While election commissioner Vivek Joshi raised objection to the revised Form 6 format on May 16 this year, Sandhu endorsed it on Aug 13, well after Supreme Court had upheld the SIR process. Their concerns were later echoed by opposition parties led by Congress, which alleged that Form 6 was changed "unilaterally" by CEC Gyanesh Kumar.The EC statement Saturday, however, put on record that all three SIR orders - issued on June 24, 2025, for Phase 1 Bihar; on Oct 27, 2025, for Phase 2 in 12 states; and on May 14, 2026, for the ongoing Phase 3 in 19 states/UTs - were unanimously approved by the CEC and the two commissioners.To eliminate any scope for doubt, EC added Saturday's statement was also issued with the "approval of the full commission".The declaration required to be attached to Form 6 itself has undergone a change since it was introduced in the SIR order for Bihar. The Bihar declaration required those seeking fresh enrolment to declare their or their parents' date and place of birth and submit proof of the same from the list of 11 documents attached to the SIR order, though this list was not exhaustive. This declaration was revised for subsequent phases of SIR, introducing mapping to the last SIR instead of seeking proof of citizenship.
Article Summary: EC retains mandatory SIR declaration for fresh voter enrolment. Source: System will revert to the pre-SIR Form 6 with immediate effect in non-Sir states/UTs, including the states due for polls early next year.

Article Title: After meeting, EC says officials will visit homes of those sent notices
Article Text:
ECINET software to be audited after complaints​

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A full meeting of the Election Commission of India on Saturday - the first after reports of alleged internal differences - decided to exempt electors who have got notices for being unmapped to the last SIR or over logical discrepancies, from hearings by electoral registration officer (ERO) or assistant EROs. Instead, EROs and AEROs will visit homes of such electors to collect documents that would then be uploaded to ECINet for a final decision by the ERO.The EC also agreed to an independent audit of ECINET software though it rejected allegations that EROs were being locked out."Only in exceptional circumstances, as decided by the ERO, hearing will be held, preferably online. Any adult member of the family can be authorised by the elector to attend the hearing on their behalf, if required," the EC said in a statement after the meeting attended by CEC Gyanesh Kumar and election commissioners S S Sandhu and Vivek Joshi.EC also agreed to an independent audit of ECINET software even as it rejected allegations that booth-level officers and EROs were being kept out.Facilities for online hearing will be strengthened, while DEOs will create enough help desks and hold special camps for the poor, labourers, homeless people, and those in night shelters.The relief for electors who received notices under SIR follows criticism from affected voters and opposition that genuine citizens are being inconvenienced by discrepancies flagged by ECINET.These include name or gender mismatch; less than a 15-year gap with a parent; less than a 40-year gap with a grandparent; being one of six progeny mapped to the same parent; and less than a nine-month gap between siblings.Until now, notice recipients had to appear before the ERO at the specified time and place with documents proving eligibility to remain on the rolls. With large numbers of notices in states like Delhi, including to prominent persons, many said citizens were forced to run around to retain voting rights.EC has also denied reports that field officers were locked out of ECINET, saying role-based access exists, but agreed to an independent audit. A senior DEC-led panel will review ECINET to double-check that it complies with the provisions of the Acts and rules and submit a report to EC.
Article Summary: EC also agreed to an independent audit of ECINET software even as it rejected allegations that booth-level officers and EROs were being kept out.Facilities for online hearing will be strengthened, while DEOs will create enough help desks and hold special camps.

Article Title: PM Modi recalls 2016 surgical strikes on Mann Ki Baat, says terrorism will get decisive response
Article Text:
File photo: PM Modi in 'Mann Ki Baat'

Other highlights from Mann Ki Baat

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday recalled the 2016 surgical strikes carried out by the Indian Army across the Line of Control (LoC), saying India has made it clear that terrorism will be met with a “strong and decisive response”.Addressing the 138th episode of his monthly radio programme Mann Ki Baat , PM Modi said the surgical strikes, carried out on September 28-29, 2016, demonstrated India's resolve to respond to cross-border terrorism.“A major historical achievement of India is set to complete 10 years in just a day—the surgical strike. Ten years ago, on September 28–29, 2016, the Indian Army conducted a surgical strike on terrorist hideouts in PoJK. The world was astonished by the manner in which our brave soldiers crossed the Line of Control (LoC) to take action against terrorism,” he said.PM Modi said the operation had demonstrated a new approach to India's counter-terrorism policy.“The surgical strike boldly demonstrated a new example of India's counter-terrorism policy to the entire world. It served as our decisive response to the long-standing suffering India had endured due to terrorist attacks,” he said.“India has made it clear that terrorism will be met with a strong and decisive response,” PM Modi added.The Prime Minister also referred to the Balakot airstrike and Operation Sindoor, saying India had repeatedly sent the same message in response to terrorism.“Over the past decade, from the Balakot airstrike to 'Operation Sindoor', India has repeatedly sent a clear message: if terrorists dare to cast a hostile eye on India, they will face a befitting response,” he said.PM Modi also asserted that India was following a policy of “zero tolerance against terrorism”.The surgical strikes were carried out in response to the 2016 Uri terror attack, with the Indian Army targeting terror launch pads across the LoC.The Prime Minister also referred to the ongoing Census exercise, describing it as a “national responsibility” and saying every citizen had a role to play. He said the first phase of the Census was almost complete across all states and Union territories, with information on more than 32 crore families already recorded. He urged people to actively participate in the exercise and make use of the online enumeration facility.With October 2 approaching, PM Modi also highlighted cleanliness initiatives being carried out by communities across the country and recalled Mahatma Gandhi's emphasis on cleanliness.“October 2nd is just a few days away; it is the birth anniversary of Revered Bapu. Bapu gave us many mantras for life; cleanliness is one of them,” he said.PM Modi cited examples of youngsters cleaning a river in Madhya Pradesh, restoring old stepwells and wells in Andhra Pradesh, volunteers cleaning Mumbai beaches and young people in Delhi spreading awareness about waste segregation. He also mentioned students and local residents in West Bengal who were cleaning picnic spots.“One thing is clearly evident in all these efforts: it started with one person, then others joined in and the caravan grew. This is public participation,” PM Modi said.“Cleanliness is also the most beautiful tribute we can pay to Bapu,” he added.PM Modi also spoke about the fight against narcotics and said young people were coming together to spread awareness against drug addiction through the Nasha Mukt Yuva Abhiyan. He said millions of young people had taken a pledge to stay away from drugs and had also taken responsibility for spreading the message among others.The Prime Minister also recalled the history of the Somnath temple, saying those who sought to erase India's identity by destroying it ultimately had no existence. He said the temple continued to stand in its grandeur by the sea, blessing India with immortality.During the broadcast, PM Modi also paid tribute to late VHP leader Ashok Singhal on his birth anniversary, recalling his contribution to the Ram Janmabhoomi movement and describing his life as that of an ascetic who remained engaged with society.
Article Summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi recalled the 2016 surgical strikes carried out by the Indian Army across the Line of Control (LoC) He said the operation demonstrated India's resolve to respond to cross-border terrorism. PM Modi also referred to the Balakot airstrike and Operation Sindoor, saying India had repeatedly sent the same message.

NEW DELHI: BJP allies in the party-led ruling National Democratic Alliance (NDA) on Saturday welcomed the Election Commission of India ’s (ECI) statement in response to a media report claiming a “rift” between Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the two Election Commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise."In the recent months, the Commission has taken numerous decisions including SIR across the country. The order for the SIR issued on 24.6.2025 for all the States/UTs, starting with Bihar, followed by West Bengal and 30 other States/UTs was issued with the unanimous approval of the Commission. The same has been upheld by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India vide its order dated 27.5.2026. The schedule for SIR for 12 States and UTs was issued on 27.10.2025 and those for 19 States/UTs was issued on 14.05.2026 with the unanimous approval of the Commission. The final figure of number of electors will be known only after final publication in the remaining 12 states of Phase-III," the ECI's press note read.Following the ECI's statement, Union minister and Lok Janshakti Party (LJP) chief Chirag Paswan, among the first BJP allies to raise the issue, maintained that it was his responsibility to voice any question or concern arising in the public mind.“The concerns raised by the public regarding SIR, which came before us, were presented before the Election Commission...Today, the Election Commission has clearly stated its position on all important issues point by point. The process of SIR, the unanimous agreement of all three commissioners, and the facts related to the meeting with the Cabinet Secretary have also been clearly presented,” Paswan posted in Hindi on X.“This clarity further strengthens public trust in democracy. The Election Commission plays a crucial role in democracy, and in this way, the trust of the country's people in democracy has increased even more,” the Hajipur MP added.Andhra Pradesh chief minister and Telugu Desam Party (TDP) supremo N Chandrababu Naidu also welcomed the Election Commission’s statement, maintaining that it "reaffirmed the credibility of constitutional institutions."“Attempts to undermine global confidence in India’s democratic framework or electoral processes for short-term political gains are deeply unfortunate. Electoral outcomes reflect the people’s mandate. In a robust democracy, leadership also means accepting both victories and defeats with grace and humility. Respect for our constitutional institutions is paramount. It is the collective responsibility of leaders across party lines to uphold public confidence in India’s democratic process,” Naidu wrote.BJP national president Nitin Nabin, too, slammed at the Congress-led opposition INDIA bloc for "misleading" the public on SIR.NDA constituents such as the LJP, TDP, Rashtriya Lok Morcha, and Janata Dal (Secular), had sought a detailed response from the ECI over The Indian Express report that Election Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi had objected at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders related to the electoral roll revision process, reflecting the unease within the ruling alliance.Meanwhile, opposition parties, including the Congress, Samajwadi Party, Rashtriya Janata Dal, Shiv Sena (UBT) and the Left parties, kept up the heat on the NDA over the issue. The INDIA bloc is likely to meet in Delhi on September 30 to discuss the matter and decide its future course of action.
Article Summary: BJP allies in the party-led ruling National Democratic Alliance (NDA) welcomed the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) statement in response to a media report. The Indian Express report claimed a “rift” between Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the two Election Commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi.

'Gyanesh Kumar is only the pawn'

NEW DELHI: Priyank Kharge on Thursday hit out at the BJP for defending the Election Commission after the Form 6 row. He said that the ruling party should allow the poll panel to answer questions over alleged differences among its members on electoral-roll decisions.The Karnataka minister's remarks came after a report by The Indian Express claimed that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders linked to electoral-roll procedures and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.“Why is the BJP so desperate to defend the Election Commission instead of allowing the Election Commission to defend itself? If there is nothing to hide, let the Election Commission face the questions directly. BJP leaders should stop acting as its unofficial spokespersons. Let the Commission come before the country, answer every question, disclose every fact and clear every doubt,” Kharge wrote on X.Kharge also questioned whether the controversy was being reduced to the role of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar while overlooking wider questions about the functioning of institutions.“Looks like the Modi Sarkar is preparing to sacrifice Gyanesh Kumar at the altar.But don’t be fooled. Gyanesh Kumar is only the pawn,” he wrote.He further questioned the legal protections available to top election officials and the way power is distributed within the poll body.“The bigger question is: who designed the system, who concentrated the power and who ensured that the Chief election commissioner received legal protection from civil or criminal proceedings for acts done in the discharge of their “official duties”?”Kharge alleged that accountability should not be limited to individual officials.“Accountability cannot stop with the pawn. The two most powerful people at the top have systematically weakened democratic institutions to cling to power and shield a system of corruption and cronyism,” he said.The controversy has also drawn comments from former election commissioner Om Prakash Rawat, who said decisions of the three-member Election Commission have to be taken through consensus or a majority vote.“That is the Election Commission's system, where all three commissioners give suggestions and contribute their views on how things should be done. That is standard procedure. However, when a decision is made, it must be by consensus or by a majority vote,” Rawat said.“If two Commissioners are on one side, that forms the majority. Their objection is that while they expressed a different view, Gyanesh Kumar proceeded independently. That is the issue,” he added.Rawat, however, ruled out the possibility of cancelling elections that have already been completed.“No one can cancel an election once completed. What is done is done,” he remarked.On calls for Kumar's resignation, Rawat said a formal process would first have to be initiated.“Someone has to initiate formal proceedings. If someone moves, then the subsequent steps will be seen,” he said.Rawat also raised questions about changes to Form 6, which is used for voter registration. He said the Election Commission could not amend statutory requirements without the required approval.He explained that Form 6 has different requirements depending on the applicant's circumstances. According to him, additional details may be sought from an older person who claims to be registering for the first time.“But what the Election Commission did this time is apply the second type of form to everyone. Even if someone is 18 years old, they are now required to provide details about where their parents were and what they did. This has led to controversy, as it effectively amounts to an amendment to Form 6. The Election Commission has amended it, even though the Election Commission has no authority to amend any form. That authority rests solely with the President,” he said.The Election Commission, however, has said that all its decisions, including those related to the SIR exercise, were taken unanimously with the approval of both Election Commissioners and the Chief Election Commissioner.Meanwhile, the Congress Working Committee is scheduled to meet in New Delhi on September 29. According to sources, the meeting is expected to discuss the Election Commission controversy, the SIR exercise and the wider political situation.
Article Summary: Priyank Kharge hits out at the BJP for defending the Election Commission after the Form 6 row. Kharge also questioned whether the controversy was being reduced to the role of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. He said that the ruling party should allow the poll panel to answer questions over alleged differences among its members.

Article Title: EC faultlines have a long history, dating back to 1989
Article Text:
Election Commission of India

Poll Vote & Share your view Which internal conflict within the Election Commission do you find most concerning? Seshan vs. Gill and Krishnamurthy Gopalaswami vs. Chawla Arora vs. Lavasa Goyal's resignation 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: It is not the first time that the fault lines within the Election Commission are out in the open. The trend started from the time it became a multi-member body in 1989.Two election commissioners S S Dhanoa and V S Seigell were appointed in October 1989 and joined the poll body then led by chief election commissioner (CEC) R V S Peri Sastri. Though Sastri never publicly spoke about it, it is widely believed that the new arrangement was perceived by him as a dilution in power. By January 1990, the appointment of the two commissioners was rescinded and the EC reverted to being a single—member body.In 1993, with T N Seshan as an all-powerful CEC, the commission was once again made a multi-member body with the appointment of election commissioners M S Gill and G V G Krishnamurthy. What followed was a running feud between Seshan on the one hand and Gill and Krishnamurthy on the other. Seshan viewed the appointments as a direct assault on the independence of his office and completely refused to recognize the two new commissioners. He refused to share official documents with Gill and Krishnamurthy, barred them from attending critical meetings, and would not allocate them any office work. He openly ridiculed the election commissioners in interviews, even referring to them as “two donkeys in my office”.Interestingly, it was on Seshan’s plea challenging the govt’s decision to make EC a multi-member body that the Supreme Court had, in 1995, ruled that the election commissioners and CEC were equal in status, power and decision-making authority and that the CEC was only “first among equals”.The other internal feud in EC to recall would be one between then CEC N Gopalaswami and election commissioner Navin Chawla between 2006 and 2009. Months before he was to step down upon the end of his tenure, Gopalaswami wrote to the President of India recommending the removal of Chawla on grounds of a pro-Congress bias. In his note to the President, Gopalaswami alleged that Chawla was passing on details of EC’s meetings to senior Congress leaders, often taking “toilet breaks” during commission meetings to do so. Gopalaswami’s recommendation was however turned down by the Manmohan Singh govt and Chawla succeeded him as CEC.During the 2019 general election, the differences between then CEC Sunil Arora and then election commissioner Ashok Lavasa came to the fore, with media reports alleging that he had dissented in cases relating to complaints of alleged model code of conduct violations by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and then BJP president Amit Shah, but was overruled without the commission making his dissent noted public. EC put out a clarification that dissent notes were only made public in quasi-judicial orders passed by EC.Lavasa resigned on August 18, 2020, two years short of his tenure, and joined the Manila-headquartered Asian Development Bank (ADB) as its Vice-President.Arun Goyal was the last election commissioner to quit in the middle of his term. Though he had cited personal reasons in his resignation dated March 9, 2024, it was widely speculated that he was not on the best of terms with the then chief election commissioner Rajiv Kumar.
Article Summary: The fault lines within the Election Commission are out in the open. The trend started from the time it became a multi-member body in 1989. Two election commissioners S S Dhanoa and V S Seigell were appointed in October 1989 and joined the poll body then led by chief election commissioner R V S Peri Sastri.

Article Text:

Article Title: Asian Games Medal Tally: How two kabaddi golds helped India break back into top 10 as China pull ahead
Article Text:
India won gold medals in both men's and women's kabaddi events.

Seven medals, kabaddi gold double the highlight

Anahat, Abhay keep gold hopes alive

Asian Games Medal Tally after Day 7

Rank Nation Gold Silver Bronze Total 1 China 107 41 28 176 2 Japan 31 49 49 129 3 South Korea 16 21 36 73 4 Uzbekistan 8 17 9 34 5 Kazakhstan 8 8 19 35 6 Thailand 8 7 9 24 7 Iran 7 14 7 28 8 Bahrain 7 2 2 11 9 North Korea 5 5 4 14 10 INDIA 4 12 14 30

NEW DELHI: India returned to the top 10 of the Asian Games medal standings on Saturday after a seven-medal haul, highlighted by two gold medals in kabaddi. The country’s gold rush in the sport, along with medals in athletics, shooting and squash, took the overall tally to 30 and moved India up to 10th place.India now have four gold, 12 silver and 14 bronze medals after seven days of competition in Aichi-Nagoya.The kabaddi teams provided the biggest boost to India’s medal count, with both the women and men successfully defending their Asian Games titles. The women defeated Iran in the final before the men followed suit later in the day, maintaining India’s remarkable dominance in the sport.India also collected medals across athletics and shooting. Sawan Barwal produced one of the standout performances of the day by winning a historic silver in the marathon, while Prachi Choudhary claimed bronze in the women’s 400m.Two-time defending champion Tajinderpal Singh Toor added another silver in the men’s shot put. Toor produced a season’s best 20.64m but could not complete a hat-trick of Asian Games gold medals after Iran’s Mohammadreza Tayebise won with a Games Record 20.81m.At the shooting range, Tilottama Sen, Vidarsa Vinod and Ashi Chouksey combined to win silver in the women’s 50m rifle 3 positions team event.India also added a bronze in squash, with Joshna Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar losing 1-2 to Hong Kong’s Tang Ming Hong and Lee Ka Yi in the mixed doubles semifinal.India’s squash campaign received a major boost as Anahat Singh and Abhay Singh advanced to their respective singles finals. Both remain in contention for gold as well as qualification spots for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, where squash will make its debut.The men’s hockey team also progressed to the semifinals after beating Japan 2-0 in their final pool match.While India climbed back into the top 10, China continued to dominate the medal standings. The Asian giants have already crossed the 100-gold mark and lead the table with 107 gold, 41 silver and 28 bronze medals, taking their overall haul to 176.Hosts Japan remained second with 31 gold medals, followed by South Korea with 16 and Uzbekistan with eight.India’s seven-medal haul helped close out a productive Saturday and pushed the country back into the top 10, with the focus now shifting to converting more of the growing medal opportunities into gold.
Article Summary: India return to the top 10 of the Asian Games medal standings after a seven- medal haul. The country won two gold medals in kabaddi, taking its overall tally to 30. India also won medals in athletics, shooting, squash and hockey. China continue to dominate the medal standings with 107 gold, 41 silver and 28 bronze medals.

Article Title: Naomi Osaka heard a 9-year-old’s tennis dream in Cameroon, then made an unexpected move that could change the young player’s journey and take her closer to the biggest stage
Article Text:
Boris Becker’s Naomi Osaka comment sparks debate after former tennis star reacts to her striking Milan Fashion Week look

Naomi Osaka backs Cameroonian tennis prodigy Uma Bogso with landmark scholarship to train at Mouratoglou Tennis Academy

Scholarship detail Information Young player Uma Bogso Age at scholarship 9 years old Country Cameroon Sport Tennis Support initiative Play Academy with Naomi Osaka Training destination Mouratoglou Academy Location Biot, near Nice, France Main opportunity Professional coaching and advanced tennis facilities

A childhood dream suddenly receives global attention

Naomi Osaka gives Uma Bogso landmark scholarship

Naomi Osaka’s Play Academy expands global mission

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Naomi Osaka has had a big impact on tennis beyond her own Grand Slam career, with her Play Academy initiative to help girls access the sport. One story that stood out was that of Uma Bogso, a 9-year-old tennis player from Cameroon whose ambitions caught Osaka’s attention.The initiative did not let geography and limited resources define Uma’s opportunities, and it granted her a scholarship to train at the Mouratoglou Academy in France. The move was an opportunity for the young player to be exposed to professional coaching, high-level facilities and an international tennis environment that had previously been well beyond her regular training setup.It started with Uma idolising Naomi Osaka and dreaming of being a professional tennis player. The Cameroonian player was only 9 years old and already playing the sport with far fewer resources than many young athletes training in established tennis systems.Play Academy with Naomi Osaka provided an individual scholarship that enabled Uma to attend the Mouratoglou Academy in France. The scholarship allowed the young player to train at a state-of-the-art tennis center, work with professional coaching staff and mingle with other junior players, Play Academy said.The scholarship was important, in part, because Play Academy was established primarily to help grassroots organisations, not to regularly fund individual athletes. Therefore, Uma’s case offered a unique opportunity in the initiative and illustrated how the situation of a particular young player could be given direct attention.The opportunity also created an environment for Uma that was built around athlete development. The Mouratoglou Academy says its methodology relies on individualised coaching, listening, performance development and helping athletes progress on and off the court.Uma’s story demonstrates what a difference access can make at the very beginning of a young athlete’s development. Talent alone does not guarantee a pathway into competitive sport, especially where coaching, facilities, tournament exposure and financial resources are limited.Also, a new tennis environment can offer a 9-year-old player experiences that go beyond the improvement of individual strokes. Playing with different players can expose you to new standards of competition, new routines, and it can also show you what a longer-term pathway in tennis can look like.That wider development is in line with the philosophy of Play Academy. The initiative was launched in 2020 by Naomi Osaka, Nike and Laureus Sport for Good, with a stated aim of increasing girls’ participation in sport and supporting organisations working with girls in underserved communities.Naomi Osaka’s involvement gave Uma’s story a key connection to a player who’s felt the pressure of top-tier tennis firsthand. Osaka has four Grand Slam singles titles and has used her platform to talk about the importance of creating opportunities for girls in sport. Osaka wanted other girls to have the same opportunities and role models on their own sporting journey that she had, Play Academy said.For Uma, the scholarship was a concrete training opportunity rooted in that larger mission. Instead of just receiving encouragement, she was able to move into a professional academy environment and work with coaches who were geared to develop junior players.The Mouratoglou Academy is located in Sophia Antipolis on the French Riviera, near Nice and Cannes. Today its facilities include 33 clay and hard courts, eight indoor courts, a fitness room, sports medicine facilities, swimming pools and accommodation options for young players.The academy also says its coaching philosophy is designed to fit individual athletes, rather than to use one method. Its methodology is based on listening to players, individual coaching, development of performance and continuous assessment.So the significance of the move is not just the number of hours spent on a tennis court. A structured academy can expose a young athlete to training habits, competition preparation and routines that are hard to replicate without access to specialised facilities.Support for Uma is part of a much larger mission established through Play Academy with Naomi Osaka. Launched in Japan in 2020 with Nike and Laureus Sport for Good, the program has focused on supporting grassroots organisations using sport to create opportunities for girls.The initiative was based on a problem beyond the game of tennis. Financial, social and access barriers can make it more difficult for girls to continue to participate in sport. Play Academy has therefore adopted an approach that has included funding, capacity-building support and gender inclusive coaching and not just elite competition.Uma’s scholarship illustrated how that philosophy could intersect with an individual athlete whose circumstances were especially compelling. Going from Cameroon to a top European tennis academy was a chance to go from very little local resources to a very structured international training setting.For a player who was only 9 years old when the opportunity presented itself, the real value of it may not be in the immediate results, but in the doors it opened along the way. Naomi Osaka’s decision gave Uma’s dream a whole new context, providing a young Cameroonian tennis player with a glimpse of how far that dream could take her.
Article Summary: Naomi Osaka backs Cameroonian tennis prodigy Uma Bogso with landmark scholarship to train at Mouratoglou Tennis Academy. The initiative was launched in 2020 by Naomi Osaka, Nike and Laureus Sport for Good, with a stated aim of increasing girls’ participation in sport.

Article Title: In 1981, Chuck Leavell and his wife inherited Georgia land; decades later, Charlane grown into a 4,000-acre estate with 70% forest cover
Article Text:
PC: US Fish and Wildlife Service

How Rose Lane’s inherited Georgia land grew into the 4,000-acre Charlane estate

How Leavell turned a life in rock music into a study of forestry

PC: WSJ

How Charlane's forests became part of a working timber operation

About 70% of the 4,000 acres is forest

The old Bullard House remains part of the property

Forestry became part of Leavell's public life

For Chuck Leavell, the road to becoming a Georgia tree farmer began with land that came to his wife’s family in 1981. At the time, Leavell was already building the music career that would take him from the Allman Brothers Band to decades of work with the Rolling Stones. The inherited property was farmland, not a ready-made forestry operation. Much of the surrounding land had long been used for crops and livestock. Leavell and his wife, Rose Lane, gradually acquired neighbouring tracts and began changing the way the property was managed. As per the reports by Wall Street Journal, what started with roughly 1,000 acres eventually became Charlane Woodlands and Preserve, a 4,000-acre property outside Macon, with about 70% of the land remaining forested. Their stewardship earned recognition well beyond Georgia, with the American Tree Farm System naming Chuck and Rose Lane the National Outstanding Tree Farmers of the Year in 1999.Rose Lane inherited the original acreage after her grandmother died in 1981. The property included family land and a house, making its future a matter of stewardship as much as ownership. Rather than leaving the acreage as it was, the couple began buying adjoining parcels over the years.That expansion changed the scale of the operation. By later accounts, Charlane had reached around 4,000 acres, a substantial increase from the land Rose Lane inherited. The property is now associated with forestry, wildlife habitat and the management of Southern pine, rather than the row crops that had previously dominated parts of the land.Leavell did not arrive at forestry with formal training. He had a different profession entirely.Leavell was already an established keyboard player by the time he took on greater responsibility for the family property. His work with the Allman Brothers Band had placed him in the American rock scene during the 1970s. The connection between his two lives gradually became clearer to him. The instrument at the centre of his career was made from wood, while the land around his home was filled with trees that could be grown, harvested and used. He began reading about land management and forestry, speaking with other landowners and learning about the practical side of running a tree farm.At one point, he studied forestry by correspondence while he was on tour. The education covered areas including forest management, prescribed burning and the longer-term decisions involved in growing timber.The couple's move towards forestry made practical sense for a property that Leavell had to manage alongside a demanding touring career. Crops and livestock require regular attention, while timber operates on a much longer cycle. Charlane's forests include Southern yellow pines such as loblolly and longleaf, along with other native hardwoods. Earlier descriptions of the property also recorded slash and shortleaf pine among the trees being managed.The intention was not simply to leave the woodland untouched. Timber production became part of the property's management, with thinning and harvesting carried out as part of the forest cycle. Leavell has described the process in practical terms, including the satisfaction of knowing that trees grown on his land could eventually become lumber for someone's home.The scale of Charlane is perhaps easiest to understand through the acreage. The property grew to roughly four times the size of the land originally inherited by Rose Lane, reaching about 4,000 acres. Recent profiles put around 70% of Charlane under forest cover. That amounts to roughly 2,800 acres of woodland, although the exact acreage of forest can change with planting, harvesting and other land-management decisions.The forests are not the only feature of the property. Charlane has also been managed for wildlife, with habitat work aimed at species including bobwhite quail, deer, turkey and ducks. Prescribed burning has formed part of the approach, helping manage vegetation and maintain habitat conditions in areas intended for wildlife.There is also a much older layer to Charlane. The Bullard House, an early 19th-century farmhouse, was restored by the Leavells in the 1990s. The property developed beyond a private residence. A guest lodge was built from timber associated with the land, while other buildings have served practical purposes including workshops and accommodation. In a 2014 account, the main house was described as a roughly 6,000-square-foot home with extensive use of Southern yellow pine, from floors to walls and exposed structural elements.A separate woodworking shop became another way for fallen or harvested trees to remain connected to the property. In the earlier account, Leavell described having large sections of an old red oak milled into thick slices that could later be turned into furniture.The work at Charlane eventually extended well beyond the boundaries of the property. Leavell became involved in forestry education and conservation, writing books about forests and appearing in projects focused on trees and land management. His forestry work has also brought recognition. He was named National Outstanding Tree Farmer of the Year in 1999 and has twice been recognised as Georgia Tree Farmer of the Year. The U.S. Forest Service also made him an honorary forest ranger.That record helps explain why Charlane is more than an unusual second career for a touring musician. The property became the place where Leavell could put the forestry principles he was learning into practice, while continuing the musical career that helped make the expansion of the land possible.
Article Summary: Chuck Leavell and his wife, Rose Lane, have been named the National Outstanding Tree Farmers of the Year in 1999. Charlane Woodlands and Preserve is a 4,000-acre property outside Macon, Georgia, with about 70% of the land remaining forested. The property is associated with forestry, wildlife habitat and the management of Southern pine.

Article Title: Dale Earnhardt Jr. turned the woods of his North Carolina estate into a motorsport time capsule, keeping more than 75 wrecked race cars in a private graveyard beside a full Wild West-style town he bui
Article Text:
Earnhardt’s collection goes back to the period when JR Motorsports was competing in late models.

How race car graveyard began

Some wrecked race cars were placed around Dale Earnhardt Jr.’s property.

More cars kept arriving

One car was missing for a year

Dale Earnhardt Jr. has turned part of his property near Mooresville, North Carolina, into an unusual collection of racing history. More than 75 wrecked race cars are scattered across his estate, which includes a private “Racecar Graveyard” and a Wild West-style town called Whisky River.According to NASCAR, the idea began with cars that Earnhardt’s JR Motorsports team had damaged while competing in late-model racing. The team had spent money building the cars, so instead of sending the wrecked vehicles to be scrapped, Earnhardt began storing them in the woods around his property. Over time, the collection grew and became a place for cars with links to different moments in NASCAR racing.Earnhardt has also imagined that the collection could remain there long after he is gone. He has earlier explained that he hoped people in the distant future might walk through the woods, discover the wrecked cars and wonder why they were there. “Just like that Western town I built,” Earnhardt said, referring to Whisky River. “It will be there hopefully long after I’m gone, and somebody will walk back there and go, ‘What in the hell is this doing here? And who put it here?’ And then my name will come up, and they’ll remember me,” he added.The collection is not arranged like a conventional museum. Some cars have been used as trail markers, while others have been placed in unusual locations around the property. Earnhardt said there are also separate car parts, including sides and noses, as well as hoods hanging from trees.Earnhardt’s collection goes back to the period when JR Motorsports was competing in late models. Rather than throwing away cars after they were wrecked, the team started keeping them on the property. Earnhardt said around half of the cars in the woods were connected to his company.The wrecked vehicles did not simply sit unused from the beginning. According to Earnhardt, some were used for target practice, while others became markers along trails. As more race teams heard about his interest in old and damaged cars, the collection expanded beyond vehicles connected to his own team.One of the cars came from Brad Keselowski’s family. It had been owned by Keselowski’s father and was crashed by Dennis Setzer during a Nationwide race at Talladega. Another is one of Keselowski’s old trucks, with its front end buried in a creek.Earnhardt also managed to collect cars connected to some memorable NASCAR incidents. One example is the car Juan Pablo Montoya was driving when he struck a jet dryer at Daytona. Chip Ganassi donated that car, but with a condition that photographs of it should not be taken.Another vehicle in the collection is the Jimmie Johnson car that was penalised over its C-posts at Daytona and was wrecked early in that race.Earnhardt continued adding vehicles whenever teams were willing to give them away. In 2014, two more cars arrived after they were wrecked at Kansas. They belonged to Justin Allgaier and David Gilliland.For the Allgaier car, Earnhardt simply contacted his friend Steve Addington, who was the crew chief and competition director for owner Harry Scott Jr.’s team. Earnhardt explained why he made the request, “I know Harry Scott pretty well, so I figured if they were going to throw it away, I could at least have it.”The collection had become large enough by then that Earnhardt could not say exactly how many cars were on his property. The cars were spread across the woods, with additional parts and pieces stored in different places.That became a problem when fans started asking whether they could visit the graveyard. Earnhardt said he felt bad that people could not simply come and see the collection because it was located on his private property.“The hard part is, people want to know if there’s tours or if they can come look at it,” Earnhardt said. “So I feel kind of bad, because it’s on my property,” he added.By 2019, the collection had grown to more than 75 cars and had become known as the “Racecar Graveyard” at Earnhardt’s Dirty Mo Acres estate.The size of the collection even meant that Earnhardt could lose track of individual cars. He had said he spent about a year looking for one particular vehicle on his own property, Sporting News reported.The missing car was Wayne Jesel’s land speed car, which had been converted from an old Xfinity car. Earnhardt explained that these cars were used on airport runways and could travel more than 200 mph over a one-mile distance from a standing start."I’ve been looking for this car for about a year. Deep in the Racecar Graveyard is Wayne Jesel’s land speed car that was converted from an old Xfinity car," Earnhardt wrote on Facebook.He added that the mystery was partly because his property manager did not tell him where new cars were placed. “My property manager never tells me where he puts the new additions. That just adds to the mystery of the graveyard,” Earnhardt wrote.The collection has therefore become more than a storage area for damaged race cars. Each vehicle represents a different part of racing history, while the woods around Dirty Mo Acres have become the setting where those cars remain.Earnhardt has described the cars as vehicles that were once fast and loud but are now sitting among the forest undergrowth. Some have faded and suffered years of exposure, while others remain relatively well preserved. His website says the common link between them is that each has a story and has been placed in the graveyard because of that history.Earnhardt has also shared photographs of several cars from the collection on social media. But despite the growing number of wrecked vehicles around his property, there was at least one car he hoped would never join them- his Superman-themed No. 88 car for the Coca-Cola 600. He wanted that car to make it all the way to Victory Lane instead.
Article Summary: Dale Earnhardt Jr. has turned part of his property near Mooresville, North Carolina, into an unusual collection of racing history. More than 75 wrecked race cars are scattered across his estate, which includes a private ‘Racecar Graveyard’ and a Wild West-style town called Whisky River.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026: Ankush Panghal punches India’s first boxing medal with 5-0 quarterfinal win
Article Text:
Ankush Panghal auures India of maiden boxing medal at Asian Games

Ankush dominates first two rounds

Salimov fights back, but Ankush holds firm

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Kurash campaign ends for Indian athletes

Reigning Commonwealth Games champion Ankush Panghal delivered a commanding performance on Sunday to assure India of its first boxing medal at the Asian Games 2026, defeating Tajikistan's Nekruz Salimov by a unanimous 5-0 decision in the men's 80kg quarterfinals.Ankush controlled the contest for most of the three rounds, using his speed, sharp combinations and solid defence to establish a decisive advantage before holding off a late challenge from Salimov.The Indian boxer came out aggressively and immediately put Salimov under pressure with a combination of right hooks and crisp 1-2 punches. Ankush won the opening round unanimously, with all five judges scoring it in his favour. He continued to dictate the pace in the second round, showcasing his movement and counter-punching ability while making it difficult for Salimov to land clean shots.His powerful left hook proved particularly effective as he secured another 5-0 verdict in the second round, leaving the Tajik boxer needing a major turnaround in the final three minutes.With his tournament on the line, Salimov came out with greater urgency in the third round and looked to land heavier punches in search of a knockdown.The Tajik boxer managed to connect with a few shots and took the final round 4-1 on the judges' scorecards. However, Ankush had already built a comfortable lead and remained composed until the final bell.Four judges scored the bout 29-28 in Ankush's favour, while the fifth judge awarded him a 30-27 victory, completing a convincing 5-0 win. The quarterfinal victory guarantees Ankush at least a bronze medal, while the CWG champion will now turn his attention to the semifinals as he bids to go one step further.India's campaign in kurash, meanwhile, suffered a series of setbacks on Sunday. Vishal was knocked out in the men's +90kg quarterfinals after losing 5-0 to Thailand's Kunathip Yea-On.In the women's -57kg category, Sangita Balhara suffered a 10-0 defeat against the Philippines' Charmea Quelino in the Round of 32. Article Title: In 2003, NFL legend Drew Bledsoe quietly purchased 80 acres of Washington vineyard land; years later, his Doubleback winery had grown to 450 acres and 70 employees, earning a Wine Spectator Top 100 ra
Article Text:
Drew Bledsoe left the NFL and built a wine empire nobody saw coming (Getty Images)

Why did Drew Bledsoe start a winery after his NFL career?

How did Doubleback winery become one of Washington's most respected labels?

How big has Drew Bledsoe's wine business grown since he left the NFL?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Most NFL quarterbacks spend their final seasons worried about their completion percentage. Drew Bledsoe was thinking about cabernet sauvignon. While still under contract with the Buffalo Bills in 2003, he bought 80 acres of vineyard land in Walla Walla, Washington, the small farming town he grew up in. Nobody made much of it at the time. Years later, that quiet land purchase had grown into Doubleback, a winery sitting on 450 acres with 70 full-time employees and a Wine Spectator Top 100 ranking under its belt.Drew Bledsoe's path to wine did not start at retirement. It started much earlier, in a farmland town that most people outside Washington state would not recognize on a map. Growing up in Walla Walla, he was surrounded by agriculture. The valley's summers were hot, the nights cool, and the soil had a texture that winemakers had been quietly excited about for years.He had started developing a taste for wine during his NFL years, sharing bottles with teammates and their families after games. It grew from a casual interest into something more deliberate. By 2003, with retirement somewhere on the horizon, he made his first move, purchasing the land that would eventually become the McQueen Vineyard."When you look at facing retirement in your mid-30s, and all of a sudden the outlet for that passion and work ethic goes away, you can't just sit back in a rocking chair and be retired at 35," Bledsoe said. "I'm not a good enough golfer to play golf every day."That honesty says a lot. Bledsoe was not chasing a vanity project or a tax write-off. He was looking for something that demanded the same competitive energy that football had required of him for 14 years. Wine, it turned out, had plenty of that.When Drew Bledsoe officially retired in 2007, he returned to Walla Walla and launched Doubleback the following year alongside his wife Maura. The name was deliberate. It was a reference to coming home, to circling back to the place that shaped him before professional football pulled him away. He brought in winemaker Josh McDaniels, who had been working at the respected Figgins Family Wine Estates, to lead production.The early skepticism from the wine community was predictable. Greg Harrington, owner of Gramercy Cellars and one of Walla Walla's most recognized winemakers, admitted he was not exactly impressed when he first heard a former pro athlete was setting up shop nearby. "My first thought was, 'Yeah, just what we need,'" Harrington said. "Some former pro athlete who knows nothing about wine."That skepticism did not last. Doubleback's first vintage, a 2007 cabernet sauvignon blend, landed a Wine Spectator Top 100 ranking straight out of the gate. Bottles were priced between $90 and $120, and they sold. The winery was not trying to compete on affordability. It was competing on quality, and the critics noticed.Bledsoe later expanded with Bledsoe Family Winery, a sister label designed to offer more variety at a lower price point. Then came Bledsoe/McDaniels, a collaboration focused on small-lot, single-vineyard wines. What started as one plot of land had quietly grown into a multi-label wine operation.The numbers tell a story Drew Bledsoe himself still finds difficult to fully explain. From a single planted vineyard to more than 450 acres and 70 employees, the growth has not been accidental. He has added estate vineyards across the Walla Walla Valley, acquired the àMaurice Vineyard in the Upper Mill Creek area, and extended his reach into Oregon's Eola-Amity Hills, where 80 acres now grow Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, and Chenin Blanc."Early on, we were not thinking that we were going to have three wineries and have 60 employees," Bledsoe admitted. "We were just going to be a cool little boutique winery and hopefully make some good wine."There is something worth noting in that. Bledsoe has never oversold what Doubleback is. He has not put his name on cheap merchandise or chased mass distribution. The investment into the business, which he described as running into the seven figures, was treated with the same seriousness he gave his playing career.It shows in the reputation the label has built."It's been super rewarding to see something grow from a single vineyard that we planted with our hands to a company that has 70 employees and over 450 acres of vineyards," he said.NFL quarterbacks are often defined by what they did under pressure on Sunday afternoons. Bledsoe spent 14 seasons doing exactly that. But the second chapter he built in a Washington farming town, one row of vines at a time, might be the more lasting legacy.
Article Summary: Drew Bledsoe bought 80 acres of vineyard land in Walla Walla, Washington, in 2003. Years later, that quiet land purchase had grown into Doubleback, a winery with 70 full-time employees. From a single planted vineyard to more than 450 acres and 70 employees, the growth has been accidental.

Article Title: 30 rescued after fire breaks out in multi-storey building housing Haldiram’s outlet in Delhi’s Model Town
Article Text:
A fire broke out in a three-storey building housing a Haldiram's outlet in northwest Delhi's Model Town area





DELHI: Around 30 people were rescued after a fire broke out in a three-storey building housing a Haldiram outlet and adjoining structures in northwest Delhi's Model Town area on Friday, officials said.The fire broke out around 2pm, following which head constable Pawan, the beat officer of Model Town police station, became the first responder and alerted senior officers, news agency PTI reported.Thick smoke was seen billowing from the building, which has a basement, ground floor and three upper floors.The Delhi fire service received a call about the blaze at around 2.40pm and initially rushed four fire tenders to the spot.As the fire intensified, the DFS deployed 23 units, including a hydraulic platform, officials said.The police team evacuated occupants of the affected building as well as those in adjoining buildings, safely rescuing a total of 30 people, police said."The building has a basement, ground and three floors. On the ground and first floor there is Haldiram and on the second and third floor there is one more restaurant.The fire was on all the floors. We have searched the entire building and no one was trapped inside," a DFS officer said.The blaze, suspected to have been caused by a short circuit, broke out in a multi-storey building housing the Haldiram outlet and other establishments, PTI reported."The fire was classified as a medium fire at 3.30pm and was brought under control around 4pm," he said.Md Sajid, assistant bank manager of a private bank, said, "As soon as the short circuit happened, the guard informed us that a fire had broken out and we should evacuate the building. The fire started on the ground floor and engulfed the whole building. We used a fire extinguisher in our office to try to extinguish the fire as much as we could on an individual level."No injury or casualty was reported due to the timely police response and prompt evacuation, officials said.(With agency inputs)
Article Summary: A fire broke out in a three-storey building housing a Haldiram outlet in northwest Delhi's Model Town area on Friday. The Delhi fire service received a call about the blaze at around 2.40pm and initially rushed four fire tenders to the spot. As the fire intensified, the DFS deployed 23 units, including a hydraulic platform, officials said.

Indian athlete Baranica Elangovan won the bronze medal in the women's pole vault at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on Friday, giving India its first-ever medal in the event at the Asian Games.The 29-year-old secured the bronze with a best clearance of 4.15m. She shared the medal with Kazakhstan's Polina Ivanova, who also cleared 4.15m. The two athletes matched each other on countback, resulting in a shared bronze.Baranica began with first-attempt clearances of 3.85m and 4.00m before needing two attempts to clear 4.15m. She then attempted 4.25m but failed on all three attempts, ending her competition with the bronze medal.Her compatriot Sindhushree Ganesha exited the competition without registering a mark, while Baranica remained in contention for a medal.Baranica has also had a strong season, improving the national record twice earlier this year. She first cleared 4.22m in March and then raised the mark to 4.23m in May at Bhubaneswar. Sindhushree G later improved the national record to 4.25m in June. Baranica's season-best remains 4.23m.The pole vaulter from Tamil Nadu had suffered an ACL injury in 2020 and went through a challenging period of rehabilitation, after which she moved to the Reliance Foundation High Performance Centre in Bhubaneswar in 2023.Japan's Misaki Morota won the gold with a best clearance of 4.55m, while China's Chunge Neu took silver with 4.50m.Baranica's bronze took India's overall medal tally at the Asian Games to 23, including two gold, nine silver and 12 bronze medals.

The SP and the Congress have been engaged in a war of words over seat sharing for quite some time now. The open fight has an uncanny resemblance to how events had unfolded between the INDIA bloc allies in Bihar.Cut to the 2025 Bihar assembly elections.INDIA bloc allies - the RJD and the Congress engaged in a continuous war of words in Bihar over seat-sharing and CM face, while the BJP-led NDA managed a smooth division of seats. What started as public posturing between INDIA bloc allies ended up in public sparring between them as the divided opposition alliance was decimated in the polls.The two parties campaigned separately for most of the time as they could not agree on seat sharing. They took out separate yatras across the state. While Rahul Gandhi undertook the “Vote Adhikar Yatra,” RJD’s Tejashwi Yadav went across the state with his “Bihar Adhikar Yatra.” Ironically, it was the success of the two yatras that boomeranged on the alliance as it made seat-sharing bitter and difficult.In the run-up to the Bihar elections, Tejashwi Yadav was confident of a sweep. The Congress was also not willing to budge, guided by its improved showing in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections in the state. The two parties used pressure tactics against each other. So much so that the INDIA bloc went into the elections as a divided house despite last-minute agreements and adjustments to keep the alliance intact.Uttar Pradesh appears to be headed the same way, at least as of now. We have already seen a lot of public posturing and sparring between the leaders of the INDIA bloc partners. Both the Congress and the SP have repeatedly claimed that the opposition’s fight against the BJP can be led only by their respective leaders.The SP and Congress contested the 2024 Lok Sabha polls together in Uttar Pradesh and won 43 seats between them, with the SP winning 37 and the Congress six. The alliance also won the Faizabad seat, which includes Ayodhya, where the BJP won in 2019.And that is perhaps where lies the genesis of this power tussle. Both the SP and the Congress feel that it was their party and leader who played a greater role in the 2024 electoral success and hence want the advantage to flow accordingly in seat sharing for the assembly elections.One look at the latest broadside between the two parties and we know why seat sharing between them may not be smooth.Recently, Samajwadi Party MP from Kairana Iqra Hasan and Congress MP from Saharanpur Imran Masood, both elected in the 2024 Lok Sabha polls as part of the SP-Congress alliance, publicly pitched their respective party leaders to take on the BJP."Only Rahul Gandhi is the opposition voice across the country, which unnerves the BJP. Rahul ji has done the hard work and created a favourable atmosphere. So make no mistake, nothing is possible without Rahul ji, and no one should have any doubts about this," Masood said.Days later, Hasan responded and pitched SP chief Yadav as the key to the alliance's prospects."Only Akhilesh Yadav is capable of defeating the BJP. On its own, the Congress won't be able to achieve much," she said.Last week, Congress Uttar Pradesh in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam signalled a firm stance regarding upcoming electoral negotiations and said that any seat-sharing arrangement with the Samajwadi Party (SP) must be built on mutual respect and equal standing.Clarifying reports regarding seat distribution, Gautam claimed that formal discussions with the SP have not yet begun. While expressing open flexibility for minor adjustments, he stressed that the Congress would not compromise its organisational self-respect or dignity in any prospective deal."We have made one thing very clear. The Congress is the country's oldest party. It was the Congress that led the freedom struggle. Any alliance formed will be based on mutual respect; there will be equal partnership and dignity. Sure, we can show some flexibility; there might be minor adjustments, but we cannot compromise on our dignity," the Congress leader said.The contrasting assertions come despite messages of unity from both sides of the divide. Akhilesh is riding high on SP’s Lok Sabha success in Uttar Pradesh. The Congress, which is trying hard to revive its lost electoral fortunes, does not want to compromise on its expansion plans in one of the most politically important states.The problem is that both the parties are wooing the same social base in the state - minorities, Dalits, women, youth. Akhilesh is missing no opportunity to expand his PDA’s - Pichda Dalit and Alpsankhyak - base by making concerted attempts to include Pandits, Aadhi aabadi (women) and other social groups. The Congress is also wooing the Brahmins, the Dalits and the women in a big way.What the two bickering allies don't realise that there are several other parties who are also reaching out to the same social base. For instance, Mayawati and Chandrashekhar Azad are also going all out to woo Dalits. Then there is Owaisi, who has already put both the parties in a Catch22 situation by offering them an alliance against the BJP. Owaisi's proposal is like a double-edged sword for the two parties. If they accept his offer, the BJP will gun for them.If they reject the offer, Owaisi will use the rejection to rally the Muslims against them.The Samjawadi Party and the Congress may do well to learn lessons from the Bihar debacle before it’s too late. Lok Sabha elections and assembly elections are two very different games and success in one does not automatically translate into success in another. There are numerous instances to show that alliances which did well in Lok Sabha elections failed in assembly elections. Maharashtra is a case in point. The Maha Vikas Aghadi of the opposition parties - Congress, Shiv Sena and the NCP did very well in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, putting the BJP on the backfoot. But a year later in 2025 - the opposition alliance was decimated by the BJP in the assembly elections. So, Akhilesh and Rahul need to decide if they want to keep on flexing muscles at each other or unite in time to pose a challenge to the BJP.
Article Summary: The Samajwadi Party and the Congress have been engaged in a war of words over seat sharing for quite some time now. The open fight has an uncanny resemblance to how events had unfolded between the INDIA bloc allies in Bihar. The SP and Congress contested the 2024 Lok Sabha polls together in Uttar Pradesh and won 43 seats between them.
