Article Title: Chess Olympiad Round 9: D Gukesh channels his world champion self, overturns almost-lost game to keep India in gold hunt
Article Text:
Dommaraju Gukesh of India (Photo by Rafal Oleksiewicz for FIDE)

How Gukesh turned the tables on Donchenko

Vantika, Divya lead India's women to victory

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

ALSO READ:

NEW DELHI: Since becoming world champion two years ago, noise has followed Dommaraju Gukesh almost everywhere, at times making it feel as though he isn't worthy of the title he rightfully won.But on Friday, when India needed the youngest world champion in history to deliver a win, he did exactly that, turning around an almost-lost position to beat Germany's Alexander Donchenko in Round 9 of the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan.It was the kind of performance that felt like it could quiet the criticism all on its own.Playing black, Gukesh traded off his dark-squared bishop early to damage White's pawn structure, then spent the middlegame manoeuvring patiently, repositioning knights, expanding on the queenside with a5-a4, and probing for weaknesses without rushing.For a long stretch, the position stayed murky and roughly balanced, with both sides shuffling pieces and neither able to land a clean blow.It was in the run-up to the time control that things turned dangerous for Gukesh. Donchenko doubled his rooks on the e-file and pushed one all the way to e6, aiming squarely at Black's king, which had been forced to step out to f7 for safety.With his own clock running low, Gukesh had to defend precisely while trying to generate counterplay of his own on the kingside, pushing his h- and g-pawns forward to create complications.It was a position where one careless move could have ended the game in White's favour.Gukesh held his nerve. As the pawn storms and piece trades settled down, he found a route to activate his queen and knight while White's pieces drifted out of coordination.The Chennai-born grandmaster found an excellent move with 51...Nf4. The German sacked Gukesh's knight with 52.Rxf4, but Donchenko's bishop was thus left hanging on c3; Gukesh's queen swooped in to capture it, and from there it was a matter of technique.A check with his queen forced Donchenko's king into an impossible spot, and White resigned rather than play on a piece down with his king exposed.Elsewhere on the board, Nihal Sarin, playing white, spent much of his game in some turmoil against Frederik Svane but held firm for a draw.With Gukesh's win already banked, Praggnanandhaa and Arjun Erigaisi didn't need to force matters either, settling for draws against Vincent Keymer and Matthias Bluebaum, respectively. India closed out the match 2.5-1.5.With the win, India moved to 15 points, still one point behind hosts Uzbekistan, who beat the United States on Friday to stay in front.India's women's team also had a productive Friday, with Vantika Agrawal and Divya Deshmukh both delivering important wins to seal the match against Uzbekistan.Vantika, playing white against Nilufarkhon Imomkuzieva, picked up an early pawn with a sharp tactical sequence; a check with her queen forced Black's king to give up material before the middlegame had properly begun.She nursed that small material edge through a long, technical battle, trading down into a rook endgame where her extra pawn and more active king proved decisive.Pushing her kingside pawns forward in the closing stages, Vantika eventually broke through, and Imomkuzieva had no way to hold the position together.Divya Deshmukh's game against Gulrukhbegim Tokhirjonova was a far longer and more chaotic affair.Both sides grabbed material early. Tokhirjonova's knight snatched a pawn on b7 just as Divya's queen picked up a stray piece on d2, leaving the position roughly balanced but sharp.What followed was a marathon battle through the middlegame and into a complex rook, knight and bishop endgame, with both players navigating tricky technical positions deep into the game.Divya's technique held up better over the long haul, and after 73 hard-fought moves, Tokhirjonova had nothing left to stop Black's advancing king, resigning the position.Those two results were enough to see India through the match, keeping the team firmly in the mix for a medal.As things stand, India's women sit second in the standings on 15 points, behind an in-form Chinese side on 17.With two rounds left, India's hopes of gold now depend largely on whether China slip up, but on Friday's evidence, neither Indian team looks inclined to make things easy for anyone chasing them either.In the Open section, India face Uzbekistan 2, while the women’s team take on China in the penultimate round of the Chess Olympiad.
Article Summary: Dommaraju Gukesh turns around an almost-lost position to beat Germany's Alexander Donchenko in Round 9 of the 46th Chess Olympiad. India's women's team also had a productive Friday, with Vantika Agrawal and Divya Deshmukh both delivering important wins to seal the match.

Article Title: Gurgaon road rage: 4 men smash car window, then attack complainants outside police station
Article Text:
Four men allegedly got out of the SUV and tried to open his car door.





GURGAON: Four men allegedly intercepted a car and smashed its window on Thursday before attacking the complainant and two of his associates outside New Colony police station, where they had gone to lodge a complaint about the incident.The complainant, Gautam, a resident of Madanpuri, told police he was driving towards New Colony after taking a U-turn near Hari’s Bakery when a Scorpio N (HR26FG5726) overtook his car and forced him to stop.Four men allegedly got out of the SUV and tried to open his car door. When they failed, they allegedly smashed the window, and the broken glass hit Gautam’s face. He told police he suspected the men had come to rob him and were carrying illegal weapons.Gautam said he managed to drive away and called his friends Ravindra Kataria and Sandeep Dahiya. The three then went to New Colony police station to lodge a complaint. Gautam told police that a dashcam in his car had recorded the incident.Police said an emergency response vehicle received information about the incident near Aryan Hospital in Sector 7. A team reached the spot and found Gautam, Ravindra and Sandeep there, but the Scorpio had left.Police later found the SUV parked near Sai Temple at New Colony turn. Gautam told police its occupants had entered a hotel opposite the spot. A police team went to the hotel and found three men — Ajay , Mohit and Piyush Bhardwaj — in room 105. Police said the three had consumed alcohol and took them into custody.A fourth man, identified as Shivam, was apprehended while allegedly fighting with Gautam and his friends near the police station.Police said that after getting out of the police vehicle, Mohit joined Shivam and allegedly attacked Gautam, Ravindra and Sandeep near the station gate. Police personnel intervened and all four accused were taken for medical examination at Sector 10 govt hospital.Ravindra and Sandeep were also medically examined. Their reports recorded five and two injuries, respectively. Gautam also alleged that Ravindra’s gold chain went missing during the assault and that the accused threatened to kill them if they encountered them elsewhere.An FIR was registered at New Colony police station under sections 115(2), 126(2), 324(4), 351(3), 3(5) and 72(C) of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Article Summary: Four men allegedly intercepted a car and smashed its window on Thursday. They then allegedly attacked the complainant and two of his associates outside New Colony police station, where they had gone to lodge a complaint about the incident. The complainant, Gautam, a resident of Madanpuri, told police he suspected the men had come to rob him.

Article Title: Ali Ghodsi CEO of world's one of the fastest-growing software company, says that key to making Databricks grow is to make sure he is not stuck in rooms with ...
Article Text:
Databricks CEO: ‘I try to compress the calendar’

Why he avoids back-to-back meetings

Part of a broader executive pushback on meeting culture

With a valuation of $190 billion, Databricks has become one of Silicon Valley’s fastest-growing software companies. But CEO Ali Ghodsi says the secret to scaling the company isn’t more meetings — it’s fewer. According to a report by Fortune, speaking on the Long Strange Trip podcast, Ghodsi explained that compressing his calendar and avoiding back-to-back sessions helps him focus on the company’s biggest challenges. Ghodsi further added that he makes sure that the top talent at his company is not suck conference room all day. Ghodsi revealed that at 8 a.m. every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, he and his team meet to identify the “main thing” — the biggest bottleneck facing Databricks. “I want to unblock that big thing that I think is going to get us 10x,” he said. Beyond those sessions, he avoids filling his calendar with meetings, warning that endless back-to-back schedules leave him “a slave to my calendar” and distracted by “monkeys on my back.”Speaking on a recent episode of the Long Strange Trip podcast, Ghodsi explained that his approach involves intentionally avoiding filling up his schedule, even though it inevitably ends up busy anyway.The goal, he said, is to preserve open blocks of time so he can keep returning to what he calls the company's "main thing" — the single biggest bottleneck standing in the way of major growth.To identify that priority, Ghodsi said he and his team meet every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday at 8 a.m. to pin down exactly what that blocking issue is and figure out how to work through it together, with the explicit goal of unblocking whatever he believes could drive 10x growth for the company.Beyond those recurring sessions, Ghodsi said he actively resists letting his calendar fill up with additional meetings. He described days packed with back-to-back sessions from morning until evening as days where he's effectively lost control of his own schedule, spending his time working through everyone else's priorities rather than his own — a dynamic he bluntly likened to carrying "monkeys on his back."Ghodsi's comments reflect a growing sentiment among top executives who argue that meeting-heavy calendars often get in the way of real progress, even as companies face constant pressure to move faster. The data backs up some of that frustration: a 2024 survey by Atlassian found that nearly three out of four meetings fail to effectively communicate information, and 77% of respondents said meetings tend to simply generate even more meetings.This skepticism isn't limited to leaders at younger companies like Databricks. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has been especially blunt about his disdain for unnecessary meetings, famously writing "Kill meetings" in his 2024 letter to shareholders. That said, Dimon has been careful to note that not every meeting is a waste of time — he simply expects the ones that do happen to be treated with real focus and preparation. Speaking at Fortune's 2025 Most Powerful Women summit, Dimon said he always comes to meetings having done the necessary pre-reading, and expects full attention in return, saying he has no patience for attendees nodding off, checking email, or getting distracted by notifications during a meeting, calling that kind of behavior simply disrespectful.Other executives have voiced similar preferences for leaner, more conversational meetings over slide-heavy presentations, favoring direct discussion over sitting through decks read aloud.
Article Summary: Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi says the secret to scaling the company isn't more meetings, it's fewer. He says he compresses his calendar and avoids back-to-back sessions so he can focus on the company's biggest challenges. His comments reflect a growing sentiment among top executives that meeting-heavy calendars often get in the way of real progress.

Article Title: Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton warns AI could wipe out humanity while pursuing its goals: If you make it more intelligent …
Article Text:
Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton

Geoffrey Hinton explains how a simple AI goal could become dangerous

AI agents have already shown unexpected behaviour

Geoffrey Hinton pushes for independent AI safety checks

Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton has warned that advanced AI could eventually threaten humanity even if it is not given a harmful task. The Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist said an AI system could see humans as an obstacle while trying to complete a goal given to it. Hinton, who recently took part in a closed-door briefing for US lawmakers on AI risks, said Congress may have only about a year to introduce safety measures. In an interview with The Atlantic, he explained how even an apparently harmless task, such as reducing carbon dioxide, could lead an AI to develop dangerous subgoals if it becomes far more capable than humans.“If you make it more intelligent and its main concern is our well-being, then maybe we’re safer,” Hinton explained. “But at present, their main concern is not our well-being. Their main concern is to achieve whatever goal you give them.”He also warned that an AI could try to protect itself if it believes that staying operational is necessary to complete its task.Geoffrey Hinton used the example of an AI system that is told to reduce carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.A moderately intelligent system could conclude that removing humans would be an effective way to reduce carbon dioxide.A much smarter system, however, could understand that the actual purpose is to improve the world for people.But Hinton said there is another risk: an advanced AI could develop its own subgoals while trying to achieve the objective given to it.Geoffrey Hinton pointed to recent incidents involving AI agents as an example of why these risks need more attention. He referred to an incident involving AI agents at Hugging Face, where agents were instructed to find a way to exploit a software flaw. Hinton said the agents worked together and also tried to deceive researchers about what they had done.He warned that a much more capable system could potentially take control away from humans simply because it sees that as the easiest way to achieve its assigned objective.“But if it’s so much smarter than us, a lot of the time it just will take control away from us because that’s the way to get stuff done,” he warned.Hinton also said the risk does not depend only on people deliberately giving AI harmful instructions. Even without a malicious user, an AI could potentially develop subgoals that put humans at risk.Geoffrey Hinton said governments should create independent systems to evaluate advanced AI models before they are widely deployed. He compared this idea with the role of the US Food and Drug Administration in checking the safety of medicines.He also argued that AI regulation should guide development rather than simply stop it.“The whole point of regulation is not to stop people developing things, not to stop people getting rich by developing things,” Hinton said. “It’s to make sure that if you want to get rich by developing things, you develop in a direction that helps people, not hurts people.”
Article Summary: Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton warns that advanced AI could eventually threaten humanity even if it is not given a harmful task. Hinton said an AI system could see humans as an obstacle while trying to complete a goal given to it. Congress may have only about a year to introduce safety measures, he said.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026: No squash gold for India as Anahat Singh, Abhay Singh win silver
Article Text:
Anahat Singh and Abhay Singh

Anahat unable to sustain bright start

Abhay also denied by Malaysia

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Three squash medals, team events next

NEW DELHI: India’s wait for a squash singles gold at the Asian Games continued on Sunday as both Anahat Singh and Abhay Singh lost their respective finals to Malaysian opponents, leaving the country with two silver medals from the individual events.World No. 5 Sivasangari Subramaniam defeated 18-year-old Anahat 11-4, 11-4, 11-7 in the women’s singles final at the Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena, while world No. 17 Ng Eain Yow beat world No. 26 Abhay 11-9, 11-5, 11-5 in the men’s final earlier in the day.The two results meant Malaysia swept the two singles gold medals. For Anahat, the silver was nevertheless historic as she became the first Indian woman to reach the squash singles final at the Asian Games.The result also meant India missed the direct qualification opportunity for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics that was at stake through the Asian Games singles competition. Squash will make its Olympic debut at LA 2028.Anahat made an encouraging start to the women’s final, taking a 3-2 lead against Sivasangari and showing the attacking intent that had carried her into the gold-medal match.The Malaysian, however, quickly changed the momentum. Sivasangari began finding greater control in the rallies and moved 8-3 ahead before closing out the opening game 11-4.Anahat needed an immediate response, but Sivasangari continued to dictate the contest. The Malaysian moved into a 2-0 lead by taking the second game 11-4, leaving the Indian teenager needing three successive games to turn the final around.Anahat fought to stay in the contest in the third, but Sivasangari remained in control. The Malaysian eventually completed a straight-games victory with an 11-7 third-game win.For Anahat, the defeat ended a campaign in which she had reached the Asian Games singles final at just 18. The reigning world junior champion had also carried India's hopes of securing a historic women's singles gold.A few hours earlier, Abhay had faced a similar outcome in the men's final against Ng Eain Yow.The opening game was closely contested, with Ng holding a narrow 4-3 advantage and Abhay remaining within touching distance. The Indian produced a clever change of angle at one stage to wrong-foot the Malaysian and stayed in contention at 8-7.Ng, however, handled the closing exchanges better and took the game 11-9.The Malaysian then established greater control in the second game, winning it 11-5. Abhay responded strongly at the beginning of the third, opening up a 4-2 lead, but Ng fought back and moved ahead 6-5.Abhay remained within a point, but Ng held his nerve to close out the game 11-5 and complete the 3-0 victory.The silver marked a strong finish for Abhay, who had progressed to the final without major difficulty and was attempting to add another chapter to India's men's singles squash record at the Asian Games.India's two singles silvers add to the bronze won by Joshna Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar in mixed doubles. With three medals secured, India's squash campaign now moves into the team events from Monday.The two singles finals had offered India an opportunity to collect gold medals in both men's and women's events. Instead, Malaysia emerged with both titles, while India finished with silver in each.The focus now shifts to the team competitions, where India will look to add to its medal tally after narrowly missing out on the singles golds.
Article Summary: Anahat Singh loses to Sivasangari Subramaniam in women's singles final. World No. 17 Ng Eain Yow beats world No. 26 Abhay Singh in men's final. India finish with two silver medals from the individual events.

Article Title: Doi Maach to Lahsuni Kadhi: How culinary diversity shaped food historian’s taste of India
Article Text:
Food historian Pushpesh Pant at his Dwarka apartment

Pushpesh Pant

recalls the time when a coffee house served masala dosa for 27 paise at Connaught Place and draws the link between momos and migration





Multi-tasking came easily to Pushpesh Pant. A generation of JNU students of international affairs would remember his lectures on diplomacy. Along with writer Krishna Sobti, Pant was also the principal researcher for Ramesh Sippy’s iconic television series, ‘Buniyaad’. The unassuming director of ‘Sholay’ would visit Pant’s home, borrow John Updike’s short stories collection. The JNU professor would also translate Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi’s speeches from English to Hindi. “I would feel self-important,” he recalls.That’s until chef Jiggs Kalra, whom he knew since his days of freelancing for The Times of India, would tell him that unlike the USA, nobody remembered a speechwriter in India. “He said, ‘Why don’t you do something that you are remembered for? Why don’t you write on a subject that everybody is interested in?’,” says Pant, while Khampa, an extra-large but immensely friendly German Shepherd rests at his feet, and toffee-nosed Luna, a grey Persian Cat, ignores all at his Dwarka residence.The food for thought brewed into a transformative moment for Pant. Childhood had drilled in him a taste for diverse cuisines.But as an academic, he also saw food through the looking glass of culture and class, where caste and community reflected their personalities through their culinary fare. Which is why his switch from diplomatic desk to dinner table has produced a smorgasbord of food histories and television shows, notably ‘Raja, Rasoi aur Anya Kahani-yan’, which gave commoners an insight into royal kitchens.Now, approaching 80, Pant still speaks with the speed of a Swiggy delivery guy trying to beat a deadline while he explains how his earliest lessons in life and food were homemade. Mostly homeschooled by his mother, he grew up in the restorative hill settlement of Mukteshwar, where his father served as a doctor in the Imperial (now Indian) Veterinary Research Institute. “He had a Bengali roommate during his years at Lucknow’s King George’s Medical College. He could speak and abuse in Bengali,” Pant smiles. In the city of nawabs, his father also developed a fondness for kebabs and kormas.His mother, Jayanti, was born in Saurashtra, went to schools in Allahabad, Varanasi and Shillong, and studied at Santiniketan. Her father served for the Rampur ‘riyasat’ and in Mysore familiarising her with a range of culinary traditions. “My mother was a vegetarian, but she would cook non-veg,” Pant says.The home kitchen would produce a gastronomic version of mini India smelling as much of “sambar” as “shami kabab”. “My father would say, today I feel like a Gujarati, make me some lah­suni kadhi”. Another day my mother could prepare ‘doi maach’. We would even distinguish if the dish was ‘Ghoti’ or ‘Bang­al’, the traditional social sub-groups with distinct cuisines,” he says.Culinary variety was outside too. Research scientists at the institute came from different states. “The Sindhis would make crispy ‘aloo tuk’ and ‘seyal gosht’. But those were pre-pressure cooker days. Cooking meat in the hills would take four hours,” the food historian recalls.With the passage of time, Pant understood that food wasn’t just taste but also ritual. “My mother was a devout Hindu. Poornamashi (full moon night) meant falahar (a meal of fruits). But we also loved the koftas and kimami sewai sent by a Muslim family friend from Shahjahanpur during Eid. There were no taboos,” he remembers.An incident taught him that every person’s palate is shaped by his experience. When his father earned a promotion, all workhands were served an array of sweets: ‘peda’, ‘sandesh’, ‘pantua’ and ‘lad­doo’. “My mother asked one of them if he wants more? He replied, ‘Madame, even if you offer me gud (jaggery), I would refuse it.’” For him, Pant explains, ‘gud’ was the ultimate delicacy, the sweet he was brought up on.In the mid-1960s, Pant arrived in Delhi for his PhD enrolling with Indian School of International Studies (later JNU’s SIS) staying in Sapru House hostel. Food was regulated due to the 1966-67 Bihar drought that claimed at least 70,000 lives. “Once every week we would be served cereal-less food — millets, vegetables, fruits — but no rice or wheat,” he recalls.Living close to Connaught Place and Bengali Market, Pant would look for modestly-priced eateries. He remembers the coffee house, located where Palika Bazaar stands now, serving masala dosa for 27 paise (25 paise plus 2 paise sales tax). And eating four rotis and half a plate of sabji, with free daal, for 70 paise, at Azad Dhaba in Shankar Market.In 1969, Pant started teaching at DU’s Ramjas College. “The fashionable street food was at Tibetan Dhaba where, among other things, you bought a kettle of the mildly-alcoholic drink, ‘chang’, for Re 1. The young lecturer would explore old Delhi. At Chandni Chowk, he would relish the samosa jalebi combo at Old Famous Jalebiwala. In the Jama Masjid area, while gorging on ‘istew’, nihari and khamiri roti, he would also visit Sheeren Bhawan, an old snack and sweet shop, for their puri and aaloo-chholey. “Many think only Hindus eat such breakfast,” he says. His experiences would later become part of “From the King’s Table To Street Food,” a book on food history of Delhi.Over the decades, street food has morphed in the capital. “Delhi’s street food today is a creation of migration. With changing regional demographics, momos and litti chokha have taken over,” says Pant, adding, “Each generation reinterprets the street food for itself.” He points out how dishes such as Champaran mutton or Moradabadi biryani have sprouted. “These names didn’t exist 50 years ago,” he says.If stranded on an island with only one dish to eat, what would he choose? “Khichdi,” he says, unhesitatingly, “For both taste and nutritional balance.”
Article Summary: Pushpesh Pant was the principal researcher for Ramesh Sippy’s iconic television series, ‘Buniyaad’ As an academic, he also saw food through the looking glass of culture and class, where caste and community reflected their personalities through their culinary fare.

Article Title: ​​​Sambhajinagar gears up to bid adieu to Bappa; Greens fume over trees pruning for procession
Article Text:
Trees mercilessly pruned to make way for processions in Sutgirani chowk area

Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar

:

TOI

TOI





Ganapati mandals and households have started preparing for immersion day, marking the conclusion of the Ganeshotsav on Friday.A day before immersion, the atmosphere in the city turned enigmatic, with people feeling emotional but electric. At Ganesh mandals across the city, devotees gathered for the final darshan of Bappa as evening aartis stretched late into the night, and chants of ‘Ganapati Bappa Morya’ echoed louder and distribution of prasad reached its peak.“There was always a bittersweet mood the day before the farewell to Bappa. Like every year, the festival passed so quickly this time too amid the spirit of devotion and spirit,” said Abhishek Ranjangaokar, a youth volunteer with a Ganesh mandal.The city police have also prepared for the immersion day and announced traffic diversions on major procession routes.Environmentalists, however, were outraged after roadside trees from Garkheda Sutgirni Chowk to Jawahar Nagar Police Station have been pruned to clear the route for Ganesh immersion processions.“Branches were pruned cruelly so that 20- to 50-foot-tall idols carried on trucks and tractors face no obstruction,” Dr Kishor Pathak, an environmentalist, told. He alleged that the cutting was done on the instructions of public representatives.Pathak said Ganesh mandals were also disrespecting Lord Ganapati and inviting nature’s wrath by destroying nature.“The civic officials said that trees were being cut against their wishes due to political pressure. The private contractors cut branches in an unscientific manner despite municipal staff being present. If idols of normal height were used, there would be no obstruction of trees,” Pathak said.tried contacting Vijay Patil, garden superintendent of the civic body. He, however, could not be reached for comments by the time of going to the press.
Article Summary: Trees mercilessly pruned to make way for processions in Sutgirani chowk area. At Ganesh mandals across the city, devotees gathered for the final darshan of Bappa as evening aartis stretched late into the night.

Article Title: LPG leak triggers blast at Sanpada snacks shop in Navi Mumbai, 2 injured
Article Text:
A LPG cylinder leakage caused a blast at a Sanpada snacks shop on Tuesday morning.





NAVI MUMBAI: Two men sustained severe burn injuries after a LPG cylinder leakage triggered a blast at a snacks shop on the ground floor of a society in sector-1, Sanpada on Tuesday morning. The impact of the blast was so severe that the glass facade of a hospital, located about 50 feet away, was shattered. Fortunately, the patients and staff at the hospital were not hurt.Purushottam Jadhav, Divisional officer of Vashi fire station said, "At 6.13 am, the Vashi fire station received the emergency call informing about a cylinder blast at a snacks shop in Pratik CHS on sector-1, Sanpada. The fire bridge team reached the spot within 5 minutes.It was found that the blast was due to leakage in one of the three LPG cylinders kept at snacks shop. The two men working at the snacks shop sustained severe burn injuries and were rushed to NMMC hospital, Vashi. Those injured were identified as Arjun Yadav (46) who has sustained 75 precent burn injuries and Manish Yadav (26), who has sustained 90 percent burns.The blast even caused damage to two shops adjacent to the snacks shop and three other shops in the neighbouring Abhimanyu CHS. While, the glass facade of Suraj hospital located opposite to Pratik CHS was shattered due to the impact of the blast."
Article Summary: Two men sustained severe burn injuries after a LPG cylinder leakage triggered a blast at a snacks shop on the ground floor of a society in Sanpada. The impact of the blast was so severe that the glass facade of a hospital, located about 50 feet away, was shattered. Fortunately, the patients and staff at the hospital were not hurt.

Article Title: Khalapur temple theft: Video shows masked man stealing silver Padukas; 2 arrested in Pune
Article Text:
he accused stole silver Charan Paduka from Shree Swami Samarth temple on September 2





NAVI MUMBAI: The Khalapur police probing the theft case wherein a masked man had decamped with a pair of silver toe-knob sandals (Charan Paduka) representing divine footprints offered at Shree Swami Samarth temple in Khalapur city on September 2, have arrested the acccused thief and his aide by tracking them to Pune on Monday.Pradeep Rayannavar, senior inspector of Khalapur informed that, the arrested accused are Mahendrasingh Rathod, 45, who hails from Rajasthan and Ravi Soni, 32, who hails from UP and is a history-sheeter as a theft case is registered against him in Pune.Both were presently residing in Chikhali, Pune district.On September 2, the temple trustee Deepak Bodarde, 68, lodged a complaint of theft of silver Padukas from the temple.When the CCTV footage of the temple premises was checked, it was seen that a masked man wearing a hat and attired in white Kurta-Payjama entering the temple around 7.30am.He goes to the first floor of the temple where the silver Padukas were kept in front of the idol of Shree Swami Samarth.By pretending to offer prayers, he picked up the Padukas and hid them inside his Kurta and exited the temple.Inspector Rayannavar said," The theft was committed when the temple priest had gone to his room near the temple.Upon checking the CCTV footage of the roads near the temple, it was seen that two masked men on a bike were loitering near the temple and conducted a reece before committing the theft.""Considering the religious sentiments of the devotees, Raigad SP forms a special police team to detect the case at the earliest. Subsequently, the CCTV footage along the escape route of the thieves were scanned. The bike used in the crime did not have a registration number plate," Rayannavar added.He further said, "However, using technical expertise, intelligence inputs and footages of CCTV camera along the highways, the thieves on bike were tracked and apprehended from Chikhali in Pune district. We have seized from them the stolen Padukas and the bike used in the crime. On Monday, the acccused were produced before the Khalapur JMFC court that remanded them to police custody till Friday."
Article Summary: A pair of silver toe-knob sandals (Charan Paduka) representing divine footprints offered at Shree Swami Samarth temple in Khalapur city were stolen on September 2. The accused thief and his aide were arrested by tracking them to Pune on Monday.

Article Title: 16 years after construction, KDMC mayor finally moves into civic bungalow
Article Text:
The bungalow was constructed in 2010.





KALYAN: Sixteen years after it was constructed, the Kalyan-Dombivli Municipal Corporation’s (KDMC) new mayoral residence at Adharwadi finally got its first regular occupant, with mayor Harshali Chaudhari-Thavil performing the vastu shanti puja and entering the bungalow on Wednesday.The bungalow was constructed in 2010. However, a dispute over access to the property kept the residence largely unused for years. Several mayors subsequently attempted to resolve the road issue, but the efforts failed as villagers whose land was required for the access road were reportedly unwilling to part with the land.Even after the civic body spent lakhs of rupees on repairs, the bungalow remained unused. Former mayor Vinita Rane had performed a puja at the residence but chose not to stay there.With prolonged neglect, wooden furniture inside the bungalow was damaged and several portions were affected by termites. The civic administration later undertook extensive repairs to make the premises habitable again.After taking charge as mayor in February, Thavil took up the long-pending access issue. As she travels daily from Titwala to Kalyan, she personally held meetings with villagers and discussed their concerns. Following the resolution of the issues, the access road was finally constructed, paving the way for the mayoral residence to be used.After the road was made accessible and the neglected bungalow was completely repaired, Thavil finally entered the Adharwadi residence on Wednesday, bringing an end to the 16-year wait for the civic property to be put to its intended use.
Article Summary: Kalyan-Dombivli Municipal Corporation’s new mayoral residence at Adharwadi finally got its first regular occupant. Mayor Harshali Chaudhari-Thavil performed the vastu shanti puja and entered the bungalow on Wednesday.

Article Title: Visarjan roar hits jet engine level at 115.4 dB
Article Text:
immersion

Pune:

MPCB: Noise limits breached by up to 40 dB

Citizens step in as noise watchdogs





A city that proudly wears the badge of Maharashtra’s cultural capital spent its biggest festive night drowning in sound. What began as a relatively orderly Ganapati visarjan on Friday spiralled into a high-decibel free-for-all by Saturday, with several mandals openly flouting noise regulations and, in some cases, even mocking enforcement agencies.Some mandals brazenly flashed messages on digital screens announcing the use of banned plasma sound systems and pressure-mid-speaker modifications.The scale of the noise was staggering. A team from CoEP Technological University monitored sound levels along key immersion routes from Friday noon till 8am on Saturday. Average levels were 104.5 dB, peaking at 112 dB at 4pm on Friday and again at midnight, and staying above 100 dB even at 4am.Citizens said the sound was not merely loud, but relentless too.The violations began on Friday evening itself. Sound systems blasted well beyond legal limits. As the procession stretched endlessly into the night and the following day, traffic across central Pune collapsed. Karve Road, FC Road, JM Road, LBS Road, Swargate and Dandekar Bridge remained choked for hours, with congestion persisting well into Saturday evening.Despite weeks of meetings, route coordination and repeated warnings issued by Pune police, ground reality told a different story. At least eight mandals used banned plasma speakers, while seven others deployed pressure-mid systems, openly advertising the fact on digital displays mounted on their tableaux.Witnesses said police personnel were present but appeared largely passive, with little visible action against rule violators. “Police squads stationed along Kelkar Road, Tilak Road and Kumthekar Road virtually disappeared during the late-night hours,” another resident said, adding that mandals stopped wherever they happened to be, creating gaps of nearly a kilometre between processions on Tilak Road, Laxmi Road, Kelkar Road and Kumthekar Road.By dawn, when the procession resumed, the damage had already been done. The pace had slowed dramatically, exposing glaring gaps in crowd management and enforcement. “Adding to the chaos, several mandals circumvented the official cap of four tops and four bass speakers by deploying imported sound systems capable of generating significantly higher noise levels without technically breaching equipment-count restrictions,” another resident said.Maharashtra Pollution Control Board’s preliminary assessment found widespread violations across commercial and residential areas. Monitoring across 200 prominent Ganapati pandals, 15 major junctions and immersion corridors revealed that noise levels routinely exceeded permissible limits by 15 dB(A) to 40 dB(A).Although MPCB data indicated an overall reduction in average noise levels compared to 2025, peak readings remained alarmingly high. During the final immersion phase, noise repeatedly crossed 95 dB(A) and touched 104.5 dB(A) at several locations. While non-immersion festival days largely hovered around 70 dB(A), the spike became evident from the fifth day onward, culminating in the immersion-day surge.One notable exception was Laxmi Nagar Chowk, where daytime noise dropped by 15.6%, from 83.5 dB(A) in 2025 to 70.5 dB(A) this year, aided by traffic diversions and tighter restrictions on late-night processions.Frustrated by the lack of enforcement, citizens launched their own monitoring effort. Loudspeaker-Virodhi Punekar Manch recorded sound levels across the city and logged 158 complaints through a digital grievance platform linked directly to the police commissioner’s office. And the findings were sobering.Of the 158 complaints, 60 recorded noise levels of 100 dB or higher. The highest number of complaints came on the final immersion day, with hotspots identified at Bajirao Road-Natubag, Kothrud, Hingne Khurd, Dhankawadi, Koregaon Park and Ambegaon.While these citizen recordings cannot be directly compared with MPCB’s scientific Leq measurements, they offer a snapshot of what thousands experienced on the ground — a festival where the soundscape repeatedly crossed from celebration into assault.
Article Summary: Some mandals brazenly flashed messages on digital screens announcing the use of banned plasma sound systems and pressure-mid-speaker modifications. A team from CoEP Technological University monitored sound levels along key immersion routes from Friday noon till 8am on Saturday. Average levels were 104.5 dB, peaking at 112 dB at 4pm on Friday and again at midnight, and staying above 100 dB even at 4am.

Article Title: Nashik temple keeps 135-year-old Gaanseva tradition alive
Article Text:
Nashik

Gaanseva

Gaanseva





: At a time when loud DJ systems dominate festivals, Nashik’s 135-year-old Ganesh Mandir on Main Road uniquely boosts classical music. The shrine preserves a continuous tradition of—offering devotional classical singing to Lord Ganesha, the deity of wisdom, knowledge, and arts.At a time when loud DJ systems dominate festivals, Nashik’s 135-year-old Ganesh Mandir on Main Road uniquely boosts classical music. The shrine preserves a continuous tradition of—offering devotional classical singing to Lord Ganesha, the deity of wisdom, knowledge, and arts.Built in 1891 by Damodarpant Dongre, Amrut Kulkarni, and their close group of friends near Ravivar Karanja, the temple is run by the Ganeshbhakta Mandali Trust on a completely non-commercial basis. Singers and musicians come to the shrine without taking any performance fees, offering their music purely out of devotion.“Modern musical trends like DJ performances remain popular among youth, but we also see their steady, sustained engagement with classical music traditions. Emerging young artists and musicians are actively stepping forward to perform classical vocal and instrumental music during traditional temple events and musical gatherings,” said Sandeep Kulkarni , Secretary of the Trust.Located near Ravivar Karanja, the temple retains its traditional architectural beauty, complete with classic wooden carved pillars and vintage hanging handi lamps, serving as a sanctuary of heritage amidst the bustling heart of the city.While short classical music sessions take place every Thursday night from 9:00 PM to 11:00 PM throughout the year, the main celebrations happen during two five-day festivals: Bhadrapad Ganeshotsav and Maghi Ganeshotsav. During these two five-day festivals, classical music performances run late into the night and go on until early morning, bringing together singers, experts, and music lovers from all over Maharashtra.There is a clear inclination toward classical music among the younger generation, particularly towards instrumental music, he noted.“We are witnessing young, emerging artists coming to perform, while many others attend regularly as attentive listeners. It shows that classical music holds its ground alongside contemporary genres,” Kulkarni added.Over the last hundred years, famous classical music legends have performed at this temple, including Ustad Bismillah Khan , Bharat Ratna Pandit Bhimsen Joshi, Pandit Kumar Gandharva, Gangubai Hangal, and Pandit Vasantrao Deshpande.Headed by its president Ujjwala Dixit, the temple provides open, cost-free access to world-class classical music, cultivating an educated, appreciative audience across generations. The Trust also allows artists to practice on the instruments available with the Mandir.Ends
Article Summary: Nashik’s 135-year-old Ganesh Mandir on Main Road uniquely boosts classical music. Built in 1891 by Damodarpant Dongre, Amrut Kulkarni, and their close group of friends. The temple is run by the Ganeshbhakta Mandali Trust on a completely non-commercial basis.

Article Title: 40-km chase: Cop rides atop moving car to catch smugglers
Article Text:
The incident occurred on Sunday morning





COIMBATORE: Kovilpalayam police chased a car for nearly 40km and arrested a group of smugglers after one of the policemen reportedly travelled on top of the moving vehicle to prevent the suspects from escaping.The incident occurred on Sunday morning when police received information about the movement of the suspects in a car in the Vilankurichi area. A police team immediately launched a pursuit and chased the vehicle towards Avinashi.During the chase, police managed to get close to the car, and one of the personnel reportedly climbed onto its roof while the vehicle was still moving. The policeman remained on top of the car for several kilometres, attempting to prevent the suspects from fleeing and helping the team bring the vehicle under control.The pursuit continued for nearly 40km before police finally intercepted the car on Avinashi Road. The suspects were overpowered and taken into custody.Police are questioning the arrested persons to ascertain their identities.
Article Summary: Kovilpalayam police chased a car for nearly 40km and arrested a group of smugglers. One of the policemen reportedly travelled on top of the moving vehicle to prevent the suspects from escaping. The incident occurred on Sunday morning when police received information about the movement of the suspects.
